entries.lesson_core_move: Express a periodic continuous-time signal in trigonometric Fourier series form by organizing its DC term and sine and cosine harmonics at integer multiples of the fundamental angular frequency.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Trigonometric Fourier Series Form
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the trigonometric Fourier series template and identify the DC term, cosine harmonics, and sine harmonics at integer multiples of $\omega_0$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show the canonical trigonometric Fourier series form and label the role of the DC term, the cosine coefficients $a_k$, the sine coefficients $b_k$, and the harmonic index $k$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the simplest periodic case with only the DC term and the first harmonic so the learner sees $a_0/2$, $a_1\cos(\omega_0 t)$, and $b_1\sin(\omega_0 t)$ in the same template.
paragraph_plan: State that a periodic continuous-time signal is represented as a DC component plus sinusoidal harmonics at integer multiples of the fundamental angular frequency.
Present the full series once and point out how $a_0/2$, $a_k$, $b_k$, and $k\omega_0$ map to the template.
Explain that $k=1,2,3,\dots$ indexes the harmonics and that each harmonic carries both a cosine term and a sine term.
Close by previewing that the next steps will fill this template term by term.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction compact and direct. The goal is recognition of the template, not coefficient derivation or Fourier theory beyond the form.

sections.section_title: Writing the DC Term and First Harmonic Terms
sections.learning_goal: Place the DC term and the first harmonic terms with the correct $a_0/2$ factor and $\omega_0$ frequency.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the expression that correctly combines the DC term and first harmonic terms from given values of $a_0$, $a_1$, and $b_1$.
distractor_plan: Omit the $1/2$ factor on $a_0$.
Put the first harmonic at $2\omega_0$ instead of $\omega_0$.
Swap the sine and cosine coefficients.
Drop one of the first-harmonic terms or give it the wrong sign.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write the DC term and first harmonic terms of the trigonometric Fourier series for a signal with $a_0=6$, $a_1=4$, and $b_1=-2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the constant term is $a_0/2=3$ and that the first harmonic is $4\cos(\omega_0 t)-2\sin(\omega_0 t)$ before combining them into one expression.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete fill-in after the template: only the constant term and the $k=1$ pair are used.
solution_step_plan: Identify the DC contribution and halve $a_0$.
Place the cosine coefficient on $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and the sine coefficient on $\sin(\omega_0 t)$.
Keep the signs of the coefficients exactly as given.
Combine the terms into one partial trigonometric Fourier series expression.
practice_variation_axes: Change the numerical coefficients while keeping only $k=1$.
Flip the sign on the sine coefficient.
Include or omit one of the first-harmonic terms.
Vary the signal description while keeping the same term placement task.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the arithmetic simple and the emphasis on term placement. Do not introduce higher harmonics or coefficient derivations.

sections.section_title: Writing Sine and Cosine Terms at Higher Harmonic Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Match higher harmonic coefficients to the correct frequency $k\omega_0$ and keep each cosine-sine pair tied to the same $k$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the expression that correctly writes the higher-harmonic terms for the given $a_k$ and $b_k$ values.
distractor_plan: Use $\omega_0$ instead of $k\omega_0$ in the trigonometric arguments.
Pair a coefficient with the wrong harmonic index.
Omit one of the sine or cosine terms at a harmonic.
Mix terms from different harmonic indices in the same pair.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write the second- and third-harmonic terms of the trigonometric Fourier series for a signal with coefficients $a_2=-1$, $b_2=5$, $a_3=2$, and $b_3=-4$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that each coefficient pair stays with its own harmonic index, giving $-\cos(2\omega_0 t)+5\sin(2\omega_0 t)+2\cos(3\omega_0 t)-4\sin(3\omega_0 t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the same template beyond the first harmonic by adding multiple higher harmonics while keeping the index-frequency pairing rule unchanged.
solution_step_plan: Read the harmonic index from each coefficient pair.
Match $a_k$ and $b_k$ to $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$.
Preserve each coefficient's sign and pair the terms within the same $k$.
Combine the higher-harmonic terms as one partial series contribution.
practice_variation_axes: Change which higher harmonics appear, such as $k=2$ and $k=4$.
Include a missing sine term or a zero coefficient.
Vary signs and coefficient magnitudes.
Mix a harmonic with a nonadjacent index to test pairing.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize index matching more than arithmetic. The main error to avoid is placing the correct coefficient on the wrong harmonic.

sections.section_title: Writing the General Trigonometric Fourier Series Sum
sections.learning_goal: Compress the full trigonometric Fourier series into one DC term plus a summation over all cosine and sine harmonic pairs.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the compact full-series expression that matches the expanded harmonic terms.
distractor_plan: Start the summation at $k=0$ instead of $k=1$.
Leave one of the trig families out of the sum.
Put $a_0$ inside the summation instead of outside.
Use the wrong harmonic argument, such as $\cos(t)$ instead of $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write the full trigonometric Fourier series for a periodic signal with DC term $a_0/2$ and harmonic coefficients $a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,a_3,b_3$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how the individual harmonic terms collapse into the compact sum $a_0/2+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left[a_k\cos(k\omega_0 t)+b_k\sin(k\omega_0 t)\right]$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This closes the lesson by replacing enumerated harmonic terms with the general summation form.
solution_step_plan: Start with the DC term outside the sum.
Write the cosine and sine contributions as a paired summand indexed by $k$.
State that the sum runs over all positive integers.
Verify that the explicit harmonic terms match the compact summation.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of explicitly listed harmonics before the summation.
Present a partial series with missing higher-order terms.
Vary the sign pattern of the coefficients.
Ask for the compact form from an expanded expression.

sections.handoff_notes: End by unifying the lesson's fixed pattern into the general compact form. Do not add derivations or coefficient calculations.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the cosine coefficients $a_k$ by integrating a periodic continuous-time signal against each cosine harmonic over one period to measure its contribution to the trigonometric Fourier series.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Cosine Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Introduce $a_k$ as the cosine-harmonic weight of $x(t)$ and show how to compute it by projecting onto $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$ over one period.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the cosine coefficient $a_k$ is the projection of a periodic signal onto $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$, so the learner can write and interpret the coefficient integral without extra scaffolding.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a signal that is exactly one cosine harmonic, $x(t)=A\cos(k\omega_0 t)$, so the integral should recover the amplitude $A$ for the matching index.
paragraph_plan: Recall that the trigonometric Fourier series separates a periodic signal into a DC term, cosine harmonics, and sine harmonics, and explain that $a_k$ measures the cosine part at index $k$.
State the coefficient formula over one period and connect it to projecting $x(t)$ onto $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$.
Use orthogonality to show why nonmatching cosine and sine terms integrate to zero, while the matching cosine term survives.
Finish with the one-term base case $x(t)=A\cos(k\omega_0 t)$ to show the coefficient returns the amplitude and confirm the normalization.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation projection-first and minimal; no practice questions belong in this section.

sections.section_title: Setting Up the Integral for a Cosine Coefficient
sections.learning_goal: Set up the cosine-coefficient integral for a concrete periodic signal and keep the setup aligned with the requested harmonic index.

question_policy.answer_format: One exact symbolic integral setup for $a_k$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which expression correctly sets up $a_k$ for a given periodic signal over one period?
distractor_plan: Use the wrong harmonic in the cosine factor, such as $\cos((k+1)\omega_0 t)$.
Omit or alter the normalization factor $\frac{2}{T_0}$.
Use only part of a period instead of one full period.
Replace the cosine test function with $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$.
Forget to substitute the given signal inside the integral.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=4+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-2\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ with period $T_0$, write the integral that computes $a_1$ and substitute the signal into it.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Write the correct coefficient integral with the right limits and integrand, then expand the signal linearly without evaluating the integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from the general coefficient rule to one concrete signal and one requested cosine index.
solution_step_plan: Identify the target coefficient $a_1$ and the one-period integration interval.
Write $a_1 = \frac{2}{T_0}\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T_0} x(t)\cos(\omega_0 t)\,dt$.
Substitute the given $x(t)$ and distribute the integrand across its terms.
Leave the result as the fully set-up expression ready for later evaluation.
practice_variation_axes: Change the target harmonic index $k$.
Swap in a different mix of cosine, sine, and DC terms in $x(t)$.
Use a different period interval or phase origin while keeping one full period.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section to the setup only; later sections should do the actual evaluation.

sections.section_title: Computing a Matching Cosine Harmonic Coefficient
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate a cosine coefficient when the signal contains the matching cosine harmonic and let orthogonality isolate the amplitude.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Which value of $a_k$ comes from a signal that contains the matching cosine harmonic?
distractor_plan: Use the amplitude of a different harmonic index from the signal.
Incorrectly include the DC term in the coefficient value.
Return zero by ignoring the matching cosine term.
Miss the normalization from the cosine-squared integral.
Confuse the cosine coefficient with a sine coefficient.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=2+5\cos(3\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)$, compute $a_3$ by integrating over one period and using orthogonality to isolate the matching cosine harmonic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the matching cosine term survives the projection and that the coefficient equals its amplitude.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Carry the setup through to a full computation, with one matching cosine term that produces a nonzero coefficient.
solution_step_plan: Write $a_3$ as the projection integral against $\cos(3\omega_0 t)$.
Split the signal into the DC term, the matching cosine term, and the sine term.
Use orthogonality to eliminate the DC and sine contributions.
Evaluate the remaining cosine-squared integral and read off $a_3=5$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the matching harmonic index.
Change the amplitude of the matching cosine term.
Add or remove nonmatching cosine or sine terms.
Ask for a different coefficient of the same signal.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the computation short and show that the matching harmonic survives unchanged after projection.

sections.section_title: Computing a Zero Coefficient for a Nonmatching Harmonic
sections.learning_goal: Show that a nonmatching cosine coefficient is zero because the projection has no surviving term.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Which coefficient is zero because the signal has no matching cosine harmonic?
distractor_plan: Return the amplitude of a nonmatching cosine term as if it were the target coefficient.
Use the wrong harmonic index and mistakenly match the present cosine term.
Report a nonzero value from the DC term.
Apply the sine-coefficient formula instead of the cosine-coefficient formula.
Treat every cosine term as if it contributed to the target coefficient.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=1+4\cos(2\omega_0 t)+3\sin(\omega_0 t)$, compute $a_3$ and show why every term vanishes when the target cosine harmonic does not appear.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the projection integral is zero because no term in the signal matches $\cos(3\omega_0 t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Replace the matching cosine term with a nonmatching one so the same projection collapses to zero.
solution_step_plan: Write $a_3$ as the projection integral against $\cos(3\omega_0 t)$.
Split the signal into its DC, cosine, and sine parts.
Apply orthogonality to each term with the target harmonic.
Conclude that every contribution is zero and therefore $a_3=0$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the nonmatching harmonic index.
Add or remove a DC term.
Include extra sine terms that still vanish.
Keep the target harmonic absent while varying amplitudes.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the zero result come from orthogonality, not from arithmetic simplification alone.

sections.section_title: Computing Cosine Coefficients of a Harmonic Sum
sections.learning_goal: Extract several cosine coefficients from a harmonic sum by applying linearity and orthogonality term by term.

question_policy.answer_format: One exact ordered tuple of cosine coefficients.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which ordered tuple gives $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4$ for a periodic signal that is a sum of cosine harmonics?
distractor_plan: Shift the coefficients to the wrong harmonic indices.
Treat the DC term as if it were one of the cosine coefficients.
Drop the zero coefficient for the missing harmonic.
Flip the sign on one of the harmonic amplitudes.
Collapse multiple coefficients into a single summed value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-4\cos(2\omega_0 t)+5\cos(4\omega_0 t)$, compute the ordered cosine coefficients $(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)$ by applying linearity and orthogonality term by term.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Extract each requested coefficient from the sum, keep the matching term for each index, and record the zero coefficient for the missing harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from a single target coefficient to a whole cosine-harmonic sum, where linearity determines several coefficients at once.
solution_step_plan: Write each requested coefficient as a projection integral against the matching cosine harmonic.
Use linearity to split the signal sum across the integrals.
Apply orthogonality term by term so only the matching harmonic remains for each index.
Read off the nonzero coefficients and mark any absent harmonic coefficient as zero.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of cosine terms in the sum.
Request a different subset of coefficients from the same signal.
Include one absent harmonic to force a zero coefficient alongside nonzero ones.

sections.handoff_notes: Show the coefficient pattern explicitly across the full harmonic sum and keep the answer tuple easy to verify.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the sine coefficients $b_k$ by integrating a periodic continuous-time signal against each sine harmonic over one period to measure its contribution to the trigonometric Fourier series.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Sine Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Introduce $b_k$ as the projection of $x(t)$ onto $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$ over one period and show that the matching sine harmonic survives the integral.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define the sine coefficient formula and show that integrating $x(t)$ against $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$ over one period measures the amount of the $k$th sine harmonic in the signal.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t)$ so the learner sees the $k=1$ coefficient return the amplitude $A$ when the matching harmonic is present.
paragraph_plan: State that the sine coefficient measures how much of the $k$th sine basis function is present in a periodic continuous-time signal.
Present the projection integral over one period and identify the role of $T$, $\omega_0$, and the harmonic index $k$.
Use the base case $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t)$ to show why the matching sine harmonic is preserved while the others cancel.
Explain that cosine terms and nonmatching sine harmonics vanish by orthogonality, then preview the worked coefficient computations.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial focused on projection and orthogonality. Do not expand into cosine coefficients or the full Fourier series form.

sections.section_title: Computing One Sine Coefficient Over One Period
sections.learning_goal: Compute $b_1$ for a signal with a target sine term plus nonmatching DC and cosine clutter.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the value of $b_1$ for a signal of the form $c_0 + c_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + c_2\sin(\omega_0 t)$ after projecting it onto $\sin(\omega_0 t)$ over one period.
distractor_plan: Drop the $2/T$ normalization factor and return the unscaled integral result.
Let the DC term contribute to the sine coefficient.
Let the cosine term survive instead of canceling by orthogonality.
Use the wrong harmonic index or the wrong sign on the target sine amplitude.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep the setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute $b_1$ for $x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)+5\sin(\omega_0 t)$ over one period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the projection integral splits into three pieces, the DC and cosine pieces cancel, and the surviving sine-square integral gives $b_1=5$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first full coefficient calculation after the tutorial, and it adds nonmatching terms that should vanish under the projection.
solution_step_plan: Write the coefficient formula for $b_1$ and substitute the given signal.
Split the integral into the DC term, cosine term, and target sine term.
Use orthogonality to eliminate the DC and cosine contributions.
Evaluate the remaining $\sin^2(\omega_0 t)$ integral and simplify to the target coefficient.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude of the target sine term while keeping the same clutter terms.
Flip the sign of the target sine coefficient.
Add another nonmatching term that should cancel.
Change the constant offset so the learner still has to ignore it.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the arithmetic simple and the emphasis on projection. The key habit is splitting the integral and discarding nonmatching terms for the right reason.

sections.section_title: Computing a Sine Coefficient for a Higher Harmonic
sections.learning_goal: Match the target harmonic index $k$ inside the integral and extract the corresponding sine coefficient while ignoring other harmonics.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the value of $b_2$ after projecting the signal onto $\sin(2\omega_0 t)$.
distractor_plan: Use the coefficient from the wrong harmonic index.
Treat the cosine term at the matching frequency as if it contributed to $b_2$.
Ignore the sign on the target harmonic amplitude.
Confuse the harmonic multiple with the base frequency and use $\omega_0$ instead of $2\omega_0$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep the setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute $b_2$ for $x(t)=1+2\sin(\omega_0 t)-3\cos(2\omega_0 t)+4\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ over one period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that only the $2\omega_0$ sine term survives the projection, so the coefficient is $b_2=4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same projection method but moves to a higher harmonic index, which forces the learner to match the correct $k$ inside the sine argument.
solution_step_plan: Write the formula for $b_2$ with $\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ in the integrand.
Substitute the full signal and split the projection into separate terms.
Cancel the DC, lower-harmonic, and cosine contributions by orthogonality.
Keep only the matching $\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ term and read off the coefficient.
practice_variation_axes: Change the target harmonic index to another higher harmonic.
Add additional nonmatching sine terms at other frequencies.
Vary the signs and magnitudes of the coefficients.
Include a cosine term at the matching frequency to test whether it is ignored.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize index matching more than arithmetic. The main error to guard against is projecting onto the wrong harmonic frequency.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Zero Sine Coefficient from Cancellation
sections.learning_goal: Use symmetry or cancellation to recognize when a sine coefficient is zero without carrying out the full integral.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the value of $b_1$ for an even periodic signal over a symmetric interval when the product with $\sin(\omega_0 t)$ is odd.
distractor_plan: Return a small nonzero coefficient from evaluating only part of the integral.
Confuse the even signal with an odd one and claim the projection is nonzero.
Treat the cosine terms as if they created a sine coefficient.
Ignore the symmetric interval and miss the cancellation argument.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep the setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Recognize that $b_1$ is zero for the even periodic signal $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)+\cos(2\omega_0 t)$ over $[-T/2,T/2]$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $x(t)\sin(\omega_0 t)$ is odd on a symmetric interval, so the integral cancels to zero without any expansion.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This replaces direct computation with a symmetry argument, so the learner can spot a zero coefficient before doing the algebra.
solution_step_plan: Write the sine coefficient integral over a symmetric interval.
Identify the parity of $x(t)$ and of $\sin(\omega_0 t)$.
Show that their product is odd, so the positive and negative halves cancel.
State the zero coefficient clearly and note that no arithmetic evaluation is needed.
practice_variation_axes: Change the even signal's coefficients while keeping the same symmetry.
Ask for a different $b_k$ that still vanishes by parity.
Include a nonmatching odd term to break the cancellation in a distractor.
Vary the symmetric interval while preserving the cancellation argument.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the cancellation argument explicit. The point is to spot zero from symmetry before attempting to integrate.

sections.section_title: Computing Several Sine Coefficients for One Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute several sine coefficients from one signal by repeating the same projection at each harmonic and organizing the results by index.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the option that lists the correct values of $b_1$, $b_2$, and $b_3$ for the signal.
distractor_plan: Swap coefficients between harmonic indices.
Drop one of the coefficients from the list.
Report only one coefficient instead of the full set.
Carry the DC term into the coefficient list or flip one sign.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No tutorial exposition in this section; begin with the worked example and keep the setup inside the example flow.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable because this section is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute $b_1$, $b_2$, and $b_3$ for $x(t)=2+6\cos(2\omega_0 t)+5\sin(\omega_0 t)-3\sin(2\omega_0 t)+4\sin(3\omega_0 t)$ over one period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the same projection rule gives $b_1=5$, $b_2=-3$, and $b_3=4$ while the DC and cosine terms vanish.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This closes the lesson by repeating the projection across several harmonics and collecting the coefficient values in one organized result.
solution_step_plan: Write separate expressions for $b_1$, $b_2$, and $b_3$ using the same coefficient formula.
Substitute the signal and isolate the matching sine term in each integral.
Use orthogonality to discard the DC term and the cosine clutter.
List the three coefficients together in harmonic order.
practice_variation_axes: Change which harmonics are present in the signal.
Add one extra nonmatching cosine term to each example.
Vary the sign pattern of the sine coefficients.
Ask for the coefficient list in harmonic order rather than one coefficient at a time.

sections.handoff_notes: Encourage a compact table or ordered list so the reader can track each harmonic cleanly. The final habit is to repeat the same projection without mixing the indices.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret $a_0$, $a_k$, and $b_k$ as the DC level and signed cosine and sine harmonic weights that describe the frequency-domain content of a periodic continuous-time signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Meaning of Fourier Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the trigonometric Fourier series as a weighted sum and map $a_0$, $a_k$, and $b_k$ to the DC term and harmonic weights.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; keep the step entirely symbolic and coefficient-focused.

tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the constant term $\frac{a_0}{2}$ as the average value of the signal, then attach one cosine and one sine harmonic at a single index $k$.
paragraph_plan: Restate the Fourier series form and point to the coefficient-basis pairing.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the DC Level from $a_0$
sections.learning_goal: Read $a_0$ as the constant offset and convert it into the actual DC level $a_0/2$ of the signal.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the worked example and practice should stay in coefficient notation.

question_policy.answer_format: One correct multiple-choice statement that interprets $a_0$ as the DC level.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which statement correctly interprets $a_0=6$ as a DC level of $3$ in the trigonometric Fourier series.
distractor_plan: Treat $a_0$ itself, not $a_0/2$, as the DC level.
Confuse the DC level with a harmonic amplitude at $k=1$.
Ignore the sign of $a_0$ when describing the offset.
Describe the constant term as a cosine or sine harmonic.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this step is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal is written in trigonometric Fourier series form with $a_0=6$. Explain what the DC level is and how it affects the whole signal.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $a_0/2=3$ is the constant offset and that it shifts every time sample equally.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from the general coefficient meaning in the tutorial to the isolated constant term and its direct numerical interpretation.
solution_step_plan: Point to the $\frac{a_0}{2}$ term in the series.
Convert $a_0$ into the actual DC level by halving it.
State that the constant term shifts the signal vertically at every time instant.
Separate the DC interpretation from the oscillatory harmonic terms.
practice_variation_axes: Different numeric values of $a_0$
Positive and negative DC offsets
Questions that ask for the average value or the constant term
Nearby cosine and sine terms that must be ignored while reading $a_0$

sections.section_title: Interpreting Signed Cosine Weights from $a_k$
sections.learning_goal: Interpret each $a_k$ as the signed weight of the cosine harmonic at frequency $k\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the target move is reading coefficient signs and harmonic indices from notation alone.

question_policy.answer_format: One correct multiple-choice statement that interprets signed cosine coefficients.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which statement correctly interprets the signs and magnitudes of $a_1$ and $a_2$ in a cosine-only coefficient list.
distractor_plan: Swap $a_k$ with $b_k$.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Harmonic Index $k$

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation short and symbolic. Emphasize that $k$ is an index label, not a separate variable, and that the cosine and sine terms share the same $k$.

sections.section_title: Matching $k$ to the Harmonic Frequency $k\omega_0$
sections.learning_goal: Map a given harmonic index to the frequency multiplier $k\omega_0$ without changing the index.

entries.lesson_title: Reconstructing a Periodic Signal from Harmonics
entries.lesson_core_move: Assemble a periodic signal by summing its DC term with sine and cosine harmonics indexed by $k$ using the fundamental angular frequency and the given trigonometric Fourier coefficients.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Reconstructing a Periodic Signal from Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the reconstruction template and identify how $a_0/2$, the harmonic index $k$, the coefficient pairs $a_k$ and $b_k$, and $\omega_0$ combine into one signal expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the reconstruction rule is entirely symbolic and coefficient-based.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show the reconstruction rule: write $a_0/2$ once, then add each available harmonic pair as $a_k\cos(k\omega_0 t)+b_k\sin(k\omega_0 t)$, keeping the coefficient-to-term mapping fixed.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a signal with only the DC term and the first harmonic pair so the learner sees the complete pattern before more $k$ values are added.
paragraph_plan: Open by naming the job: reconstruct a periodic signal from its trigonometric Fourier coefficients, not from a time-domain sketch.
State the general form and label the DC term, the harmonic index $k$, and the frequency multiplier $k\omega_0$.
Work through the base case with $k=1$ only so the learner sees $a_0/2$, $a_1\cos(\omega_0 t)$, and $b_1\sin(\omega_0 t)$ in one line.
Call out the two recurring checks: the DC term is halved, and every harmonic pair keeps its own $k$ and sign.
Close by previewing the examples, where the same rule is applied to more harmonics, missing terms, and a coefficient table.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction compact and formula-first. The goal is to establish the assembly rule and the coefficient pairing check before any worked examples.
